issues.legal_issue: The restriction on civil revision of interlocutory orders does not remove the High Court’s constitutional jurisdiction to review subordinate court orders.
material_facts: A civil suit sought a permanent injunction over agricultural land, and the trial court refused an interim injunction.
The appellate court also refused the interim injunction.
The amendment to the civil procedure revision provision made a revision unavailable against the appellate order because that order did not finally dispose of the suit.
The High Court dismissed the constitutional petition as not maintainable.
issues.conclusion: The amendment restricting revision did not affect or remove the High Court’s jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227, and the petition could not be dismissed as not maintainable merely because revision was unavailable.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 226 and 227 confer constitutional judicial-review and supervisory powers that cannot be taken away or curtailed by the amendment to Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India establishes that the High Courts’ jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 forms part of the Constitution’s basic structure. Shiv Shakti Coop. Housing Society v. Swaraj Developers recognizes that an available remedy need not be specially preserved by a grant of liberty.

predicates.challenge_to_interlocutory_civil_order: A party to a civil proceeding challenged an interlocutory order made by a subordinate court.
predicates.revision_unavailable: The party could not obtain civil revision of the order because the order did not finally dispose of the proceeding.

issues.definition: When a party challenges a subordinate court’s interlocutory civil order and civil revision is unavailable, constitutional review power remains available.

issues.legal_issue: A subordinate civil court’s judicial order may be reviewed by certiorari even when the underlying dispute is between private parties.
material_facts: The dispute was between private parties in a civil suit concerning an injunction over land.
The High Court dismissed the petition on the basis that the requested injunction was against private respondents.
The challenged orders were made by subordinate civil courts.
issues.conclusion: A writ of certiorari may be directed against the judicial act or order of a subordinate court even when the underlying dispute is between private parties; this is distinct from issuing mandamus against a private party.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, certiorari may issue to a judicial or quasi-judicial body empowered to determine rights and required to act judicially. T.C. Basappa v. T. Nagappa, Province of Bombay v. Khushaldas S. Advani, and Dwarka Nath v. Income-tax Officer support that principle. The Court explained that Ganga Saran v. Civil Judge did not foreclose certiorari review of subordinate court orders: its statement concerned issuing mandamus against a private party. Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra confirms the constitutional availability of certiorari to review inferior court decisions.

predicates.certiorari_challenge: A party sought review of a judicial decision made by a subordinate court.
predicates.subordinate_judicial_decision: A subordinate civil court made the challenged decision while determining a matter before it.

issues.definition: When a party seeks certiorari review of a subordinate court’s judicial decision, that decision is reviewable even if the underlying dispute is private.

issues.legal_issue: Certiorari may correct jurisdictional defects and specified grave legal errors, but it does not provide an appeal on the merits.
material_facts: The petition challenged subordinate courts’ refusal of interim injunctive relief.
The High Court dismissed the petition without examining the asserted errors, treating the private nature of the dispute as a bar.
The Supreme Court restored the petition for consideration under the appropriate constitutional jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: Certiorari is available for jurisdictional errors, flagrant disregard of law or procedure, or violations of natural justice that occasion failure of justice; a mere wrong decision or ordinary error is insufficient, and the High Court may not reappreciate evidence as an appellate court.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 certiorari corrects errors of jurisdiction, including acting without or in excess of jurisdiction, and may address flagrant legal or procedural violations or denial of natural justice causing failure of justice. A decision error is reviewable only when manifest and apparent on the record and accompanied by grave injustice or gross failure of justice. The Court relied on Hari Vishnu Kamath v. Ahmad Ishaque, Custodian of Evacuee Property v. Khan Saheb Abdul Shukoor, Nagendra Nath Bora v. Commissioner of Hills Division, T.C. Basappa v. T. Nagappa, and Satyanarayan Laxminarayan Hegde v. Mallikarjun Bhavanappa Tirumale. A patent error must be self-evident and not require lengthy or complicated argument.

rule.if: certiorari_proceeding and (jurisdictional_defect or flagrant_legal_or_procedural_violation or (patent_error and grave_injustice))

predicates.certiorari_proceeding: A party sought supervisory review of a subordinate court’s decision through certiorari.
predicates.jurisdictional_defect: The subordinate court acted without jurisdiction, exceeded its jurisdiction, or failed to exercise jurisdiction it possessed.
predicates.flagrant_legal_or_procedural_violation: The subordinate court flagrantly disregarded law or procedure, or violated natural justice where no procedure was specified.
predicates.patent_error: The challenged error was self-evident on the record and did not require lengthy or complicated reasoning to establish.
predicates.grave_injustice: The error caused grave injustice or gross failure of justice.

issues.definition: In a certiorari proceeding, a jurisdictional defect, a flagrant legal or procedural violation, or a patent error causing grave injustice may justify correction, but an ordinary merits error does not.

issues.legal_issue: The High Court may use Article 227 to correct serious jurisdictional failures by subordinate courts, but must exercise that power sparingly and not as an appeal.
material_facts: The challenged orders were made by courts subordinate to the High Court.
The High Court dismissed the petition without considering it under the supervisory jurisdiction that the Supreme Court held remained available.
issues.conclusion: Article 227 permits intervention when a subordinate court assumes jurisdiction it lacks, fails to exercise jurisdiction it has, or exercises jurisdiction in a manner not permitted by law, and that conduct occasions grave injustice or failure of justice; the power is not a means to correct mere errors or reappraise evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 confers judicial superintendence over subordinate courts and tribunals. Waryam Singh v. Amarnath and Umaji Keshao Meshram v. Radhikabai describe its supervisory character; Chandrasekhar Singh v. Siva Ram Singh and State v. Navjot Sandhu emphasize that it is exercised sparingly to keep subordinate courts within the bounds of their authority, not to act as an appellate court. The Court also relied on Baby v. Travancore Devaswom Board concerning intervention where material documents were not considered and that omission could lead to an opposite result.

predicates.article_227_proceeding: A party sought, or the High Court considered exercising, supervisory review of a subordinate court’s decision.
predicates.subordinate_court_jurisdictional_failure: The subordinate court assumed jurisdiction it lacked, failed to exercise jurisdiction it had, or exercised jurisdiction in a manner not permitted by law.
predicates.grave_injustice: The jurisdictional failure caused grave injustice or failure of justice.

issues.definition: When supervisory review concerns a subordinate court’s jurisdictional failure that caused grave injustice, intervention may be used to correct the failure without turning the review into an appeal.

issues.legal_issue: Constitutional review of an interlocutory order should ordinarily be withheld when the error can be corrected later, but may be appropriate when later correction is unavailable or refusal would cause serious injustice.
material_facts: The challenged orders concerned interim relief in a civil suit that remained pending.
The ordinary revision remedy was unavailable against the appellate order.
The High Court had dismissed the petition as not maintainable rather than considering whether constitutional intervention was appropriate.
issues.conclusion: Certiorari and supervisory powers are discretionary and must be exercised sparingly. The High Court should consider whether the error can be corrected at the conclusion of the proceeding and whether intervention would obstruct its progress; intervention may be warranted where later correction would be impossible or refusal would cause a travesty of justice or prolong the litigation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the exercise of Articles 226 and 227 as governed by judicial self-discipline and discretion. It recognized the legislative policy of avoiding delay from review of every interlocutory order, while preserving intervention for errors that would become incapable of correction or where refusal itself would result in injustice or prolong the dispute. Umaji Keshao Meshram and Navjot Sandhu support sparing exercise of supervisory power; the Court also referred to the principles in Ganga Saran v. Civil Judge.

rule.if: constitutional_review_proceeding and grave_injustice and (later_correction_unavailable or refusal_would_prolong_litigation)

predicates.constitutional_review_proceeding: A party sought certiorari or supervisory review of an order made during a subordinate court proceeding.
predicates.grave_injustice: The challenged error threatened grave injustice or a gross failure of justice.
predicates.later_correction_unavailable: The error could not be effectively corrected at the conclusion of the proceeding through a later appeal or revision.
predicates.refusal_would_prolong_litigation: Refusing immediate intervention would itself prolong the dispute or obstruct justice.

issues.definition: In a constitutional review proceeding, intervention may be justified where grave injustice is threatened and later correction is unavailable or refusal would prolong litigation.
